name: Longest Max Min Subsequence
description: You are given an integer sequence $$$a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_n$$$. Let $$$S$$$ be the set of all possible non-empty subsequences of $$$a$$$ without duplicate elements. Your goal is to find the longest sequence in $$$S$$$. If there are multiple of them, find the one that minimizes lexicographical order after multiplying terms at odd positions by $$$-1$$$. For example, given $$$a = [3, 2, 3, 1]$$$, $$$S = \{[1], [2], [3], [2, 1], [2, 3], [3, 1], [3, 2], [2, 3, 1], [3, 2, 1]\}$$$. Then $$$[2, 3, 1]$$$ and $$$[3, 2, 1]$$$ would be the longest, and $$$[3, 2, 1]$$$ would be the answer since $$$[-3, 2, -1]$$$ is lexicographically smaller than $$$[-2, 3, -1]$$$. A sequence $$$c$$$ is a subsequence of a sequence $$$d$$$ if $$$c$$$ can be obtained from $$$d$$$ by the deletion of several (possibly, zero or all) elements. A sequence $$$c$$$ is lexicographically smaller than a sequence $$$d$$$ if and only if one of the following holds: $$$c$$$ is a prefix of $$$d$$$, but $$$c \ne d$$$; in the first position where $$$c$$$ and $$$d$$$ differ, the sequence $$$c$$$ has a smaller element than the corresponding element in $$$d$$$.
input_specification: Each test contains multiple test cases. The first line contains the number of test cases $$$t$$$ ($$$1 \le t \le 5 \cdot 10^4$$$). The description of the test cases follows. The first line of each test case contains an integer $$$n$$$ ($$$1 \le n \le 3 \cdot 10^5$$$) — the length of $$$a$$$. The second line of each test case contains $$$n$$$ integers $$$a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_n$$$ ($$$1 \le a_i \le n$$$) — the sequence $$$a$$$. It is guaranteed that the sum of $$$n$$$ over all test cases does not exceed $$$3 \cdot 10^5$$$.
output_specification: For each test case, output the answer in the following format: Output an integer $$$m$$$ in the first line — the length of $$$b$$$. Then output $$$m$$$ integers $$$b_1, b_2, \ldots, b_m$$$ in the second line — the sequence $$$b$$$.
approach_summary: Build a Segment Tree over the array. Implement point update and associative range query operations in O(log N) time per query.

topic_editorial.title: Editorial: 2001D — Longest Max Min Subsequence [57. Segment Tree (Point Update Range Query)]
topic_editorial.summary: Range queries and updates via Segment Tree.
topic_editorial.key_invariant: The query operation is associative (e.g., sum, min, max, gcd). Any contiguous range $[L, R]$ can be decomposed into at most $O(\log N)$ canonical dyadic intervals represented by nodes in a binary tree.
topic_editorial.solution_walkthrough:
### Step 1: Tree Construction
We build a binary segment tree over array $A[1..N]$.
Each node covers a segment $[L, R]$. If $L = R$, the node stores $A[L]$. Otherwise:
$$\text{node.val} = \text{combine}(\text{left\_child.val}, \text{right\_child.val})$$

### Step 2: Point / Range Updates
To update position $pos$ with value $val$:
- Traverse down to the leaf node $[pos, pos]$.
- Update leaf value.
- Recompute ancestor values on the way back up in $O(\log N)$ time.

### Step 3: Range Query Processing
To query the associative aggregate on range $[qL, qR]$:
- If current segment $[L, R]$ is completely within $[qL, qR]$, return node value.
- If disjoint, return identity element.
- Otherwise, split and return $\text{combine}(\text{query}(left), \text{query}(right))$.
topic_editorial.complexity_analysis:
- **Time Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}((N + Q) \log N)$
  Building the segment tree takes $\mathcal{O}(N)$. Each point/range query and update traverses at most $4 \log N$ tree nodes, requiring $\mathcal{O}(\log N)$ time per query.
- **Space Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}(N)$
  A standard binary segment tree requires at most $4N$ nodes to represent elements up to index $N$.
